opener.heading: Week 10: Circus Adventures 🎪
about: A bedsheet goes over four dining chairs on Friday morning and the big top stays up until Thursday. Every day after that adds one act underneath it. She tumbles on a comforter and names her own six tricks, builds a sound desk out of the low cupboards, lifts a hundred-kilo barbell made of newspaper, draws four clown faces off her own reflection, walks a rope taped down the hall with a rice sock on her head, and catches scarves that fall slow enough to give her time. The morning builds the act and the afternoon plays it.

Thursday is the show. She draws the poster with herself as the star, delivers three of them to the doorsteps she picks, sells tickets from a box by the tent door and announces every act through a paper cone in the order she set at breakfast. Film that one end to end. The tent comes down on Thursday evening and the barbell goes out with the recycling, so the poster and four minutes of wobbly video are what is left of the week.
azlyn: Balance she can feel changing. Heel to toe along a rope, arms out sideways, a rice sock on her head that falls the moment she looks down.
Telling two close sounds apart. Seven noise-makers on one desk, eyes shut, picking the keys out from the pasta jar.
Four feelings with a face and a word each. Happy, sad, cross and surprised, pulled in a mirror and drawn on paper plates she keeps.
What heavy does to her body. Sorting the counter into two piles, hauling the barbell overhead, loading a basket until it stops moving.
Running an order she set herself. Her names on the trick cards, her numbers on the tickets, her five acts on the fridge list nobody is allowed to change.
you: Adjectives are the scaffolding for thinking
Auditory discrimination is the reading skill nobody mentions
Body awareness is a sense too
Naming a feeling reduces its intensity, and the drop is measurable
Teaching a child to notice her own body settling is a lifelong tool
What a self-portrait tells you about her thinking
shopping: Masking tape, 3 rolls (every day this week wants some)
Packing tape
A large bedsheet, or 2 single sheets
Clothespins or bulldog clips, 8
Dining chairs, 4, or a drying rack and 2 chairs
Heavy books, 8–10, plus 1 paperback for balancing
Red paper, 6 sheets
Black paper, or a black crayon
Plain paper, a stack of 20 sheets
The biggest paper or the biggest box in the house, for Thursday's poster
Cereal boxes, 5, kept flat, or paper grocery bags
Shoeboxes, 3
A cardboard box big enough for her to sit behind
Thick card, 2 sheets
Index cards, 6, or 6 pieces cut from a cereal box
Cardboard tubes, 5
Crayons
Washable non-toxic poster paint
Colored paper and a glue stick
Markers, 2, one of them fat and black
Paper plates, 4
Craft sticks, 4
Scissors (adult only)
String, 4 meters
Wide elastic, 1 meter
A jump rope or a length of clothesline, 3 meters
Chalk
Thick rubber bands, 4
Baking paper
A comb
Rice or dried lentils, 2 cups
Freezer bags, 2, if the rice and the lentils both run out
Dried pasta and a screw-top jar
Clean socks, 4, three of which are not coming back
Newspaper, a full stack
A comforter, or 3 folded blankets
Sofa cushions, 4
A laundry basket
A tray, and an upturned box for the sound desk
A saucepan lid and 2 wooden spoons
An empty plastic bottle with its lid
A bunch of keys, and a small bell
A broom, and a broom handle for the barbell
A big metal spoon
A can, a mug, a bag of flour, a full bottle and a dish towel, for the heavy-and-light line-up
A hand mirror, and a full-length mirror she can stand in front of
An umbrella, for the balance pole
A ribbon or an old belt for the sash, and a belt for the clown
Light scarves, burp cloths or thin dish towels, 3 (a square of sheer curtain or a dishcloth works)
A cardigan of yours
An adult hat
Every teddy and doll in the house
Your phone, charged, filming something most days
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 9 months this week. He pulls himself up on anything that holds still, picks a paper strip off the floor with finger and thumb, and waves at everything that waves first. He turns 9 months on Friday the 5th.

days.title: The Big Top Goes Up
days.prepTonight: Cut six sheets of red paper into long strips, and stand the big sheet, the clothespins, the masking tape and four heavy books beside the dining chairs.

opening.title: Marking Out the Ring
opening.need: 1 roll masking tape · 2 meters of string · a clear patch of floor.
steps: Push the sofa and the coffee table back to the walls with her. She picks which end of the room the ring goes in.
Hold one end of the string down in the middle and let her walk the other end round you, laying tape as she goes. The circle comes out lopsided. Leave it lopsided.
Tell her a tent goes over that circle at 9:15, then leave her to walk the line while you clear breakfast.

main.title: The Big Top
materials: 4 dining chairs, or a drying rack and 2 chairs
Red paper, 6 sheets, cut into long strips
4 heavy books to weight the edges
steps: Stand the four chairs on the tape circle, backs facing out, as far apart as the sheet will reach.
Drape the sheet over the top and clip it to the chair backs. Clips hold where a tucked edge slides off the moment she leans on it.
Ask her where the door goes. Clip that edge so she can lift it and drop it, and put it on the side you can see from the kitchen.
Tape the red strips down the outside, roof to floor, all the way round. You hold each strip, she sticks the tape.
Weight all four outside edges with the books. Nothing goes on the roof.
Tape a paper flag to the string, run it from the top of the tent to the back of one chair, and get in with her.
main.tip: It stays up until Thursday, so build it to survive her crawling in and out forty times. More clips and heavier chairs beat a neat sheet.

outside.title: Flags in the March Wind
paras: Tape three paper flags to three sticks and take them out. The wind arrives in gusts this month, so walk to the open end of the park and hold the flags up where nothing blocks them, then round the side of a building where the air goes still. She will find the windiest spot on the street before you do.

days.infant: Kreston turns 9 months today. He pulls himself up on anything that stays put. Sit him at the sofa edge, outside the ring, with a fat wad of red strips taped together at one end. He works the loose end with finger and thumb, a skill about two weeks old, and it holds him a while. Stay beside him, because a strip that comes free goes to his mouth. He waves at the flags outside. Wave back and he does it again.

second.title: The Ringmaster
second.intro: The tent has a door and nobody has been announced through it yet. The hat takes the longest, so it comes first.
materials: 1 cereal box or 2 sheets thick card
Black paper, or a black crayon (paint works)
1 sheet of paper rolled into a cone
1 wooden spoon or cardboard tube for the baton
Every teddy in the house, for the audience
steps: Cut a strip of card long enough to go round her head, tape the ends into a ring, and check it sits above her ears.
Cut a card circle wider than the ring for the brim, snip tabs round the inner hole, and tape the tabs up inside the ring. She holds, you cut.
Cover the outside with black paper, or hand her the crayon and let her do it. The patches she misses stay missed.
Roll the sheet of paper into a cone, tape the seam, and let her test her voice through the narrow end.
Tie the ribbon over one shoulder and under the other arm. She chooses the shoulder.
Line every teddy along the hallway. She walks the parade with the baton, announcing each one by name, and the parade ends inside the big top.
Let her announce you, and then be whatever she introduced you as.
second.tip: Some children never get past the cone. If the parade never happens, the afternoon still worked.

alternatives: Hat only. Skip the sash and the parade.
A megaphone each and a conversation from opposite ends of the hall.
Empty the dress-up box and make nothing at all.
outAgain: Grandparents or family, and she arrives in the hat
The park, and the flags go back out
A friend's house with the megaphone in the bag
The café with the window seat, if the wind has won

aroundWorld.title: China: Acrobatics 🎪
paras: Chinese acrobatics runs back more than two thousand years, to village harvest festivals where people showed off with whatever was to hand: plates, jars, tables and chairs. Those props are in the acts today, and a troupe will spin a stack of dinner plates on thin sticks or balance a heavy jar on a bare head.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Eat lunch in the tent the way a troupe eats between shows, bowls of noodles on the floor. Let her spin the empty bowl on the back of a wooden spoon afterwards.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Han dynasty acrobats performed with jars, tables and plates from their own kitchens.

days.krestonPM: He is the front row. At 9 months he waves, and a parade of teddies coming down the hall toward him beats any of it. Sit him propped in the tent doorway so he can watch her coming. Take the flag string down off the tent before he is on the floor near it.

insight.headline: Interoception, the sense nobody lists.
paras: Sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell get all the attention. Azlyn is also building interoception, the sense that reads her own insides: hunger, thirst, a full bladder, a heart going fast after she has run round a tent. That wiring is half built at three, so she can be starving and tell you she is fine, then come apart over a sock. You are already doing the thing that helps. Name the signal out loud when you spot it (your tummy is rumbling, that means hungry), and name the state she is in when she comes off the parade. Each label hands her a word for something she can feel and cannot yet place.

days.safety: Kreston will haul himself up on the chair legs holding the tent and bring the whole frame down on top of himself, so stay in the room while he is near it. Loose paper strips go to his mouth, so sweep them up before he is down and keep his wad taped. The books weight the outside edges and never the roof. The scissors stay with you. String at his height is a strangulation risk, so take the flag line down before he is on the floor.

days.title: Acrobats
days.prepTonight: Fold the comforter in half on the living room floor, cut six cards out of a cereal box, and stand the rice and three clean socks on the counter for this afternoon.

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Every Low Wall on the Street

opening.title: Building the Soft Floor
opening.need: 1 comforter or 3 folded blankets · 4 sofa cushions · masking tape.
steps: Drag the comforter onto the cleared floor beside the ring, clear of the four chairs holding the tent, and let her lay it out. Fold it double where she says she is going to land.
Wall the far edge with the cushions. Check what is behind her head rather than in front of her, and move the coffee table now.
Run a strip of tape along the near edge as the start line. She will test the mat by throwing herself on it, which is the test you wanted.

main.title: Six Tricks and a Bow
materials: 6 index cards, or 6 pieces cut from a cereal box
1 roll masking tape for the start line
A phone, for filming one trick
steps: Show her a move, let her try it, then ask what it is called. Write her name for it on a card in marker, big enough to read from the other side of the room.

Six moves: a forward roll, a log roll down the length of the comforter, a bridge on hands and knees, a candle on her back with her hips on the mat and both legs straight up, a jump with a half turn, and a stork balance on one foot.
Every move ends on the tape line with a bow. The bow is how she knows a trick has finished.
Lay the six cards face up. She picks the running order and performs the set from start to end.
Film the one she is proudest of and watch it back with her once.
Leave the cards on the mat. She runs the set again at 4:15 with nobody watching.
main.tip: Spot her with your hands ready and off her. A forward roll goes wrong at the moment an adult lifts her halfway through it.

outside.title: Every Low Wall on the Street
paras: Walk the usual route and stop at every low wall, curb and painted line on it. She goes along the top with a hand in yours, then without. March leaves the bottoms of walls wet and green, so pick the dry ones and expect one soaking anyway. Count the walls on the way out and see whether her number holds coming back.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months. Put him on the carpet beside the mat, off the comforter and clear of the landing end, with one cushion to pull up on. A soft thing is harder work than a hard one, and you will see him sink into the cushion, plant a hand wider and try again. He tires faster against the cushion than against the kitchen cabinet, and he wants it more.

second.title: The Beanbag on Her Head
second.intro: Three rice socks take ten minutes to make and get used every day for the rest of the week.
materials: 2 cups rice or dried lentils (flour in a double freezer bag if you have neither)
steps: Fill each sock a third full, knot it twice, and turn the cuff back over the knot. She pours, you knot.
Run a line of masking tape from one end of the hall to the other with a bend in the middle of it.
She walks the line with one sock on her head. It falls. She starts again from the beginning, and she will insist on that rule herself.
Stack the second sock on top of the first and let her find out how much less her head can move.
Add the tray held flat in both hands, with the paperback on it and one sock on her head.
Time a run with the phone and say the number out loud. Then ask for a slower one and time that.
Put a sock on your own head and let her walk you down the line.
second.tip: Arms out sideways do more for her balance than anything you can say about it. Put your own arms out and she copies without being asked.

alternatives: Three tricks instead of six, then stop.
Rice socks only, thrown and caught on the mat.
Balance a sock on your head and let her knock it off.
Cushions on the floor and a jumping game with no cards.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of the month
Whichever gallery has a floor she can sit on, if the rest is packed
The indoor play center, if it is raining sideways
The park with the low wall she liked this morning
days.krestonPM: Take him in the sling for the first half of the museum. At 9 months he pulls up on anything at knee height, so find the room with a carpeted corner or a low bench and put him down there for twenty minutes. Let Azlyn choose which room he sees.

insight.headline: Adjectives are the scaffolding for thinking.
paras: Azlyn named six moves this morning and you wrote her words down. Describing words are the tools she sorts the world with. Nouns hand her the objects, and adjectives let her hold a quality on its own, so heavy stops belonging to one can and becomes something a box, a basket and a brother can each be. Slower, higher and softer are the first measuring she does without a ruler. Feed her the ones she is missing while her body is still doing the thing: that roll was tighter than the last one. An adjective attached to something she can feel sticks better than one off a page.

days.safety: The mat lies on the cleared floor beside the ring and clear of the four chairs holding the tent, because a roll into a chair leg brings the whole frame down on her. Move the mat away from the coffee table, the fireplace and the radiator before she rolls, and check what is behind her head, not in front of her. Double-knot every rice sock and check them for leaks between goes. Loose rice on the floor is a choking hazard for a 9-month-old with a pincer grip, so sweep before Kreston goes down.

days.title: The Circus Band
days.prepTonight: Fill a screw-top jar with dried pasta, find the comb, the saucepan lid and four thick rubber bands, and stand three empty shoeboxes by the door.

opening.title: One Noise Each
opening.need: the kitchen cupboards · a tray or upturned box · her.
steps: Open the low cupboards and give her one job: find five things that make five different noises. The tray takes whatever she brings out.
Take each one in turn and make its noise once. She copies it with her mouth.
Ask her which two sound closest. Leave her answer alone and put the tray out for 9:15.

main.title: The Sound Effects Desk
materials: 1 upturned box or tray as the desk
1 comb and a sheet of baking paper
1 empty plastic bottle with its lid
Dried pasta in a screw-top jar
A bunch of keys or a bell
Masking tape and a marker for labels
steps: Set the desk on a table at her height and lay the noise-makers out in a row she decides on.
Build the two that need building: fold the baking paper over the comb to hum through, and stretch the four rubber bands across the open end of the shoebox.
Play each noise and let her say which circus act it belongs to. Write her answer on masking tape and stick it on: the drum roll, the trapeze, the clown falling over, the lion.
Sit with your back to her and call an act. She shuts her eyes and finds the right one.
Swap over. She calls the acts, you play them, and you get one wrong on purpose.
Run the whole set in order, loud to quiet, as a show for Kreston.
main.tip: Put the keys next to the pasta jar and let her work at telling them apart.

outside.title: The Birds Are Back
paras: Stand still at the end of the street and listen before you walk anywhere. Early March is when the singing starts up again, and there is more of it before nine than at any other hour. Hold up a finger for every different bird she hears.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and turns his head to a sound before he turns his body. Bang the wooden spoon on the saucepan lid at the far end of the room and watch him find you, then do it from behind him. Give him the plastic bottle, lid taped on hard and checked before he gets it. He bangs it for a few minutes, then comes back to it two or three times across the hour.

second.title: The Clown Shoes
second.intro: A clown walks wrong on purpose, and she has to work out how first. The boxes take an hour to build and the walking takes the rest.
materials: Paint, or colored paper and glue
A chair back to hold for the stand-up
1 sturdy hardcover book, for the step up
One of your cardigans and a belt
steps: Cut two slits across the top of each box, a foot's width apart. You cut, she holds the box still.
Thread the elastic through and knot it underneath so it makes a strap over the top of her foot.
Line the inside with packing tape where her heel lands, because that corner goes first.
She paints or papers them, and the colors go on big, bright and uneven.
Put them on sitting down on the carpet, with her hand on a chair back for the stand-up.
She walks a length of carpet on her own first. Then she takes a hand in yours for one step up onto a book, a turn on the spot, and the walk back.
Put your cardigan on her with the belt round the middle and stand her in front of the mirror. Give her ten minutes in front of it with nothing to do.
second.tip: Boxes with the sides left tall stay on her feet. The moment you cut them down to look neat, they fall off at every step.

alternatives: One box each and no straps. Slide them along the floor instead.
Paint the boxes today and walk in them tomorrow.
Giant shoes out of your rain boots and two pairs of socks.
outAgain: A playground you have never been to, one stop further than the usual one
The usual playground, if the new one turns out to be built for big kids
The woods, for sticks worth bringing home
Somebody's yard, if anyone will have you
days.krestonPM: The baby swing is the whole trip for him. At 9 months he holds his head steady through a proper push and spends the rest of it watching Azlyn come down the slide. Wipe the seat before he goes in, and keep his hands off the metal chains, which pull the heat out of small fingers in March.

insight.headline: Auditory discrimination is the reading skill nobody mentions.
paras: Azlyn shut her eyes this morning and picked one noise out of seven. Telling two close sounds apart is a skill of its own, and reading sits on top of it. A child who cannot hear the difference between the front of bat and the front of pat has nothing to hang a letter on, and the gap turns up in school as a reading problem when it started in the ear. Household objects beat an app for this, because the sounds are messy and she has to hold two of them side by side to choose. The two she keeps confusing are the ones her ear is still working on.

days.safety: Thick rubber bands go straight into a 9-month-old's mouth and he can reach the shoebox from standing. Count them onto the desk and count them off, and keep the desk on a table, never the floor, while Kreston is loose. Bang the saucepan lid at the far end of the room from him. The scissors stay with you. The box shoes go on carpet, never on a hard floor, never on the stairs and never near the tent chairs. Stay within arm's reach for the first walk, and hold her hand for the step up onto the book.

days.title: The Strongest Girl in the Circus
days.prepTonight: Save the newspaper, put two big cereal boxes and the packing tape on the table, and stand the broom by the door with the laundry basket emptied.

opening.title: Lifting Everything in the Kitchen
opening.need: six things off the counter · two clear patches of floor.
steps: Line up a can, an empty mug, the bag of flour, a wooden spoon, a full bottle and a dish towel.
She lifts each one and puts it in one of two piles, heavy or light. Leave both piles as she sorts them.
Ask which is the heaviest thing in the row, then hand her the can and the flour at once and let her change her mind.

main.title: The Hundred-Kilo Barbell
materials: 2 large cereal boxes, or 2 paper grocery bags
1 broom handle, or 3 paper-towel tubes taped end to end
Masking tape for the lifting line
steps: She crumples the newspaper, you pack it, until a thumb pressed into the box meets no give.
Push one end of the broom handle into each box and tape the joint round and round. That joint is the whole barbell, so use more tape than looks sensible.
Write a giant 100 on each box. Let her say the number and copy it underneath.
Tape the lifting line at the far end of the room from Kreston. Lift from the line: to her knees, to her shoulders, over her head. Count each one out loud.
Carry it the length of the room and back with the number facing out, then set it down and bow.
Load the basket with books and let her drag it by one handle. She decides how many go in and takes one out when it stops moving.
main.tip: The barbell looks enormous and weighs nothing, and she is in on the joke. Ask for a strongman face and you will get a look you have never seen before.

outside.title: Moving the Fallen Branches
paras: March storms leave the park littered. Take a strong bag and shift fallen branches into one pile at the edge of the field, biggest first. She will find one too heavy and want it anyway, so take one end and give her the other. Then ask her to sort the pile into what she can carry alone and what needs two people.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and pulls to stand, so this week he is learning what holds his weight and what comes with him. Give him the empty laundry basket upended on the carpet. It takes his weight, and he will pull up on it, drop, and go again. The drop is practice too, and he is getting better at landing on his bottom.

second.title: The Tightrope on the Floor
second.intro: The rope goes down the hallway this afternoon and stays there until Thursday. A line on the floor sets her the same problem a real tightrope does.
materials: A jump rope or length of clothesline, 3 meters (masking tape alone works)
1 umbrella, or a cardboard tube as the balance pole
One of Saturday's rice socks, or a folded dish towel
Chalk, for the same line outside
A chair back to hold at the start
steps: Lay the rope flat down the hall and tape it to the floor every half meter so it cannot roll under her foot.
Walk it yourself first, heel to toe, arms out, and say nothing about how.
She holds the chair back for the first meter, then lets go and does the rest alone. Do not walk beside her with a hand out.
Hand her the umbrella across her body in both hands. The pole steadies her, and she will feel it work.
Put a cushion either side of the middle stretch, so stepping off the rope means stepping into something soft.
Rice sock on her head for one full length. Count her steps out loud so she has a number to beat.
Chalk the same line on the path outside, coats on, and walk it where the ground is uneven.
second.tip: She will go faster to stay upright. Ask for a slow walk and count her steps, because slow is what makes her use her feet.

alternatives: Masking tape line only, no rope.
Walk the line carrying a full cup of water.
Set the cushions out in a row and jump the gaps instead.
outAgain: The neighborhood park, and the branch pile you started this morning
The field with a ball and nothing else
A walk with the chalk in your pocket for a line on every path
The corner store on the way back, and she carries the bag the whole way home
days.krestonPM: Sit him on the grass at the edge of the branch pile with one short thick stick, too fat to go far into his mouth. At 9 months he bangs two things together on purpose, and a stick on a tree root will hold him longer than a toy would. Check the ground with your hand first.

insight.headline: Body awareness is a sense too.
paras: Shut your eyes and touch your nose. The sense that got your hand there is proprioception, receptors in muscle and joint reporting where every part of you is without your eyes involved. Azlyn's version is still coarse, which is why she grips a paper cup like a hammer and misses the chair when she sits down. Weight is how the map gets calibrated. She braces for a hundred kilos, gets a broom handle and two boxes of newspaper, and adjusts. Every load she moves today sharpens that map, and a sharper map is what lets her pour her own drink next year.

days.safety: Keep the barbell and the loaded basket off her feet, and load the basket where it will be dragged rather than carried up a step. Kreston pulls to stand and will grab the broom handle mid-lift, so the lifting line goes at the other end of the room from him, and nothing gets dragged across a floor he is sitting on.

days.title: The Clown's Four Faces
days.prepTonight: Put four paper plates, the hand mirror and four craft sticks on the table, and pack the swim bag before you go up.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Hat That Won't Stay On

opening.title: The Face in the Spoon
opening.need: 1 big metal spoon · her breakfast chair · you opposite her.
steps: Hand her the spoon and let her find her own face in both sides of it. One side turns her upside down and she will go back to it.
Ask for a cross face, then a sad one, then a surprised one, and let her watch each one arrive in the spoon.
Say what her eyebrows are doing each time. Say nothing about the mouth yet, because that is the job at 9:15.

main.title: Four Faces on Four Plates
materials: 4 paper plates, or 4 circles cut from a cereal box (scissors, adult only)
steps: Four plates on the table in a row, mirror propped up where she can see herself without holding it.
Happy first. She pulls the face in the mirror, looks at it, then draws it. Leave every wobbly eye where she put it.
Sad next. Ask what the corners of a sad mouth do and let her check in the mirror before she draws.
Cross, then surprised. By the fourth she will be telling you what the eyebrows do.
Write the feeling word on the back of each plate in marker while she paints the cheeks and the nose.
Tape a stick to the back of each one, low enough for her hand, and stand all four in a mug on the table.
main.tip: Four plates and four words is plenty. A fifth face turns a set she can hold in her head into a pile she cannot.

outside.title: The Puddle Mirror
paras: Find a puddle with the sky in it and look down together. She makes the four faces over the water and watches them arrive. Wind wrecks the picture, so hunt out a sheltered one in the lee of a wall. Then let her jump in it, because a puddle she has been careful of for ten minutes becomes unbearable. Rain boots on, spare socks in the bag, swim things in the same bag.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and watches a face the way Azlyn watches the mirror. Hold him facing you and make the four faces, one at a time, with a pause after each. He will try one back, and the surprised one gets copied first because the mouth moves most. Let Azlyn do it as well. She gets a bigger response than you do.

second.title: The Hat That Won't Stay On
second.intro: One gag, repeated three times, is a whole clown routine. She has to know what comes next before it can be funny to anybody but her.
materials: 1 adult hat, or Friday's ringmaster hat
Teddies and dolls for the front row
steps: Show her the gag once. Hat on your head, bend down for the broom, hat lands on the floor behind you, and you look everywhere for it except down.
Break it into three parts and name them with her: hat on, hat off, hunting for the hat. Three is as many as she can hold.
Run it through with her, counting the parts on your fingers as they happen. Do it four or five times until she is ahead of you.
Let her add one thing of her own. Whatever she adds stays in, including the bit where the broom falls over.
She picks up a plate face at the end to show the audience what the clown feels about it.
Line the teddies up and sit Kreston at the front, propped and facing the right way. Perform the whole thing and film it without stopping.
Watch it back once and ask her which part made him laugh.
second.tip: Rehearsal is the part she loves. Running the same three beats again and again is how she learns that a story can be planned, so let her call for a sixth go.

alternatives: One gag, done four times, and nothing else.
A puppet show with the plate faces over the back of the sofa.
Photograph her pulling each of the four faces and stick them on the fridge.
outAgain: Swimming
The indoor play center, if the pool is closed for a school session
The library, a day early
Ten minutes at the park on the way back, no longer
days.krestonPM: He is in the water with you today. At 9 months he holds the rail and bobs, and he will spend the session watching the big children at the far end rather than his own hands. Both your hands stay on him. Get him out before the shivering starts, because he loses heat faster than Azlyn does and shows it later.

insight.headline: Naming a feeling reduces its intensity, and the drop is measurable.
paras: Put a feeling into words and it loses height. Researchers call it affect labeling, and in scanner studies the people who name what they are feeling show a quieter amygdala and more work happening in the language areas. Azlyn has less of that machinery built than an adult, so she borrows yours. She drew four faces this morning and has four words to go with them. Hand her the word in the middle of the wobble (you look cross, that is the cross plate) and you are lending her the part of her brain that has not finished growing. She will point at a plate before she can say the word, and pointing counts.

days.safety: Swimming this afternoon. Kreston stays within arm's reach in the water at all times, 20 minutes is plenty at 9 months, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands. Paint goes on plates and paper, never on Kreston's skin, and washable non-toxic paint only while he is mouthing everything he can reach. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: The Slow Circus
days.prepTonight: Dig out three light scarves or burp cloths, and stand a cardboard box big enough for her to sit behind by the table with ten sheets of paper in it.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: The Slowest Thing in the Room

opening.title: The Slowest Thing in the Room
opening.need: 1 scarf · 1 sock · four things she picks herself.
steps: Stand on the second stair, or hold the scarf and the sock up at full stretch, and drop both at once. She calls which landed first.
Race the scarf against four things she chooses, one at a time. She drops, you watch, she calls the winner.
Ask her why the scarf takes so long to get down. Take whatever she says and leave it there.

main.title: One Scarf, Then Two
materials: 3 light scarves, burp cloths or thin dish towels (a square of sheer curtain or a dishcloth works)
Masking tape for her standing spot
steps: Tape a cross on the floor. She stands on it, and everything happens from there.
Scrunch one scarf, throw it above her head rather than out in front, and let it come down into her hands. She will grab too early for the first ten goes.
Once she has caught five, add a clap in the middle. Throw, clap, catch.
Two scarves next, one in each hand, both thrown at once. They will be landing on the floor for a good while yet, and neither of you minds.
Throw one across her body and then the other, and let her set the speed. Say the rhythm out loud with her.
Put the basket three steps away and see how many scarves she can land in it, then move it back a step.
main.tip: Nothing here breaks, rolls under the sofa or hurts when it lands on her. Nothing gets set up and nothing gets cleared, so it is the cheapest hour of the week to run, but the scarves come up off the floor the moment you step out of the room.

outside.title: Counting the Crocuses
paras: Crocuses are up this week, purple and white and yellow in the grass under the trees, and the first dandelions are open along the sunny curb strip. Walk one street and count every crocus on it. Bring the number home and write it on the fridge with the date. Look for the fat green daffodil buds, and go back on the weekend to see which of them opened.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and a scarf is the best toy in the house for him this month. Drape one over his head and wait. He pulls it off, and the game is that you are still there. Object permanence is landing for him now, and he will hand the scarf back and lean in for another go. Stay with him the whole time it is out.

second.title: The Ticket Booth
second.intro: Tomorrow is the show and somebody has to be on the door. She builds the booth, makes the tickets and takes the orders.
materials: 1 cardboard box, big enough to sit behind
A small bell or a spoon on a jar for the counter
steps: Turn the box on its side and cut a hatch in the front, big enough to pass a ticket through. Tape the edges so nothing catches her hand.
She draws the sign. You write the words she gives you underneath, in her order and her wording.
Cut the paper into strips for the tickets. She numbers them, and the numbers go wherever she thinks.
Make the money: a stack of paper squares you cut while she stacks them, one size each for the different coins.
Set the bell on the counter. Ringing the bell means the booth is open, and she decides when.
Every person in the house lines up and orders a ticket for tomorrow's show. She takes the money, hands the ticket over and says the price out loud.
Put the tickets and the money back in the booth for the night. She needs them at the tent door tomorrow.
second.tip: Buy a ticket in character. Ask what time the show starts and take her answer as fact, because a shop works when the customer believes in it.

alternatives: One scarf, thrown and caught, for as long as she wants.
Tickets only, no booth.
Draw tomorrow's poster today, if she is already asking about it.
outAgain: The indoor play center, and the baby area for Kreston
The library, if the indoor play center has a party in it
The crocus street again, to count what opened since this morning
The park with a scarf in your pocket, if the wind is worth showing her
days.krestonPM: The baby area, and stay in it. At 9 months he pulls up on the padded blocks and drops back on his bottom over and over, which is the whole trip for him. Check the ball pit for what other people have left in it, because his pincer grip finds the smallest thing in any room.

insight.headline: Teaching a child to notice her own body settling is a lifelong tool.
paras: Azlyn goes up fast and comes down without noticing she has. The coming down is the part she can learn to feel. At the end of the scarf hour, sit on the floor with her and ask her to listen to her own breathing. Put a hand on her shoulders and ask whether they are up by her ears or back down. Her voice drops before she notices it has, so say that out loud as well. You are pointing at the recovery while it happens, which is the only time the label sticks. A three-year-old who has felt her own body settle in a calm room has something to reach for later, in a room that is not.

days.safety: Thin scarves are a strangulation risk. Nothing goes round anybody's neck, and nothing light stays on the floor once Kreston is down. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Show Day
days.prepTonight: Flatten the biggest box in the house and lean it against the wall with the crayons, check the four tent chairs are still where you need them for 1:00, and drop a dried lima bean into a cup of water for tomorrow morning.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Poster with Her on It

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Show Under the Big Top

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Props Back in the Box

opening.title: The Running Order
opening.need: 1 sheet of paper · 1 marker · the week behind you.
steps: Name the acts of the week between you: ringmaster, acrobat, strongman, clown, juggler. She will remember one you have forgotten.
She puts them in the order she wants tonight. Write the list as she says it and number the lines 1 to 5.
Stick it on the fridge at her height. That list is the show, and nobody changes it after breakfast, you included.

main.title: The Poster with Her on It
materials: The biggest paper in the house, or a flattened cardboard box
Crayons, and washable paint if she wants it
A mirror propped up in front of her
3 sheets of plain paper for the small posters
steps: Lay the box flat on the floor and tape the corners down so it cannot slide out from under her hand.
Prop the mirror in front of her and ask her to have a good look before she starts. Then step back out of her light.
She draws herself as the star of the show, as big as she wants her. Do not add an ear, a finger or a line.
Ask what the poster should say, then write her words underneath in marker, word for word, mistakes and all.
She fills the edges with the other acts, and the barbell will be bigger than the tent.
Three small posters on plain paper for delivering, then tape the big one where it faces out of the window.
main.tip: Write her words in her order even when they arrive backwards. In eight months you will read that line off a cupboard door and it will be the thing you kept.

outside.title: Delivering the Posters
paras: Walk the route with three small posters and hand them over. One through the grandparents' door, one in the corner-store window if they will have it, and one for whichever neighbor she picks. She says the time of the show at each door, and the time can change between houses. March mornings still want gloves, and she does the walk back past her own poster at a run.

days.infant: Kreston is 9 months and waves, and today three doorsteps wave back. Front-facing in the carrier for the delivering. Back home, put him on the floor beside the poster while it dries and let him flatten his hands on it. He has watched her draw all week from a distance, and a sheet of cardboard the size of the room is the first bit of it he can get to.

second.title: The Show Under the Big Top
second.intro: Everything the week made comes out at once: the tent, the hat, the barbell, the rope, the scarves, the plate faces, the sound desk and a box of tickets.
materials: The big top, still up since Friday
The ringmaster's hat, sash and megaphone
The barbell and the taped tightrope
The scarves and the four plate faces
A phone, filming the whole thing
steps: Straighten the tent and re-clip any edge that has come loose. She sets the ring out and decides where the audience sits.
Booth by the door. Everybody buys a ticket, hands it in at the tent door and gets shown to a cushion.
Pin the running order where she can see it from the middle of the ring.

She announces each act through the megaphone in the order she set this morning, then does it. Ringmaster, acrobat, strongman, clown, juggler. The acrobat act is the mat and the taped rope both, because she owns the two of them.
Sit at the sound desk and play what she calls for. Miss one cue on purpose and let her tell you off in character.
Film the whole thing without stopping, wobbles and all, with the camera down at her height.
Bow at the end. Clap for longer than feels reasonable and let her come back out for a second bow, because she will want one.
second.tip: The show runs four minutes and the setting up takes an hour. That ratio holds at every circus, and the hour is the part she enjoys.

alternatives: Half a show. Two acts and a bow.
A show for Kreston only, no filming.
Skip the show and watch the week's videos back instead.
outAgain: The hardware store, for a poster in the window and a look at the rope
The corner store, and let her deliver the last poster
The park, to run off whatever the show did not
Past the grandparents' door, to see her own poster up in it
days.krestonPM: He has a ticket and a front-row cushion. At 9 months he waves, and an audience that waves back will keep him going for the length of the show. Give him a wooden spoon of his own to bang.

insight.headline: What a self-portrait tells you about her thinking.
paras: The Azlyn on that poster has a head the size of a dinner plate, legs coming out of her chin and no body between them. Every three-year-old draws that figure, and it maps what she is attending to. Faces come first, because faces are where the information is. Count what she put in: fingers, hair, a mouth with teeth, Friday's hat. Each of those is something she has decided matters about being herself, and the list will be different by summer. Add nothing to it. A drawing you improved records your thinking, and the one worth keeping is the one that shows hers in March.

days.safety: Every prop the week made is on the floor at once, and Kreston has a pincer grip and pulls to stand. Sweep the ring for craft sticks, paper money and rubber bands before he goes in it. Take the big top down yourself, chairs last, with both children out of the room.
